title: A Week Off, a Drive to North Carolina and the Mill That Rang Back
dek: With $5,000 in savings and no contacts in hosiery, Sara Blakely drove to the mills herself, was turned away, and two weeks later got a call.

story.event: Driving to North Carolina's hosiery mills to find a manufacturer for footless pantyhose
story.summary: In 1998 Sara Blakely, a fax-machine saleswoman in Atlanta, set aside her $5,000 savings to develop footless control-top pantyhose while keeping her job. After mills refused her by phone, she drove to North Carolina and was turned away in person; about two weeks later a mill manager called to say he would help, citing his daughters. Spanx reached Neiman Marcus in autumn 2000 and never took outside investment.
paragraphs: At some point in the late 1990s, Sara Blakely took a week off from her job selling fax machines and drove from Atlanta to North Carolina, where many of the country's hosiery mills were. She had spent months ringing manufacturers without getting anywhere, so now she went in person. By her account, the mill owners asked the same three questions: who she was, whom she represented and who was backing her. Her answer to all three was Sara Blakely, and most of them sent her away.

The idea dated from 1998, when she cut the feet off a pair of control-top pantyhose to wear under new cream trousers to a party. They smoothed the line, but rolled up her legs all night. She was 27, had never taken a business class or worked in fashion, and had set aside her whole savings, $5,000, earned over seven years of selling door to door. She kept the day job. For two years she worked at night: evenings in the Georgia Tech library reading hosiery patents, visits to craft shops for fabric, and a patent application she drafted herself from a book rather than pay a lawyer thousands, though she later had one help write the claims. For a year she told almost no one, wary, she later said, of the doubt that friends and family offer out of love.

About two weeks after she got home, a call came from one of the mills. The man on the line had decided, she recalled, to help make her "crazy idea". Asked why, he said he had daughters, and they had told him it made sense. The prototype then took about a year, she said, because she meant to wear it every day and was obsessed with comfort.

In the autumn of 2000 she flew to Dallas, showed a Neiman Marcus buyer the before and after in her own cream trousers in a ladies' room, and won a place in seven of its stores. That November, Oprah Winfrey named Spanx one of her favourite things, and Blakely left her sales job around then, still packing orders herself. She never took outside investment. In 2012 Forbes valued the company at about $1 billion, all of it hers.

quote.text: I am not concerned that I have no place, I am concerned how I may fit myself for one. I am not concerned that I am not known, I seek to be worthy to be known.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius tells his students not to fret at being unknown, only at being unready. The mill owners sent Blakely away precisely because she was unknown, and she spent years making sure she would not be. Her year on the prototype answers his second sentence; the cold calls and the drive argue with his first.

reflection: Being nobody in particular is a real obstacle. The mill owners' three questions were not unreasonable: a factory has to judge who will pay, and an unknown name with no backing is a risk. Blakely could not change her answers quickly. What she could change was the quality of what she would eventually put in front of buyers, and she gave that a year.

You may know the feeling of being asked, in effect, who you are and who is behind you. It is worth noticing how much of the answer is in your hands today and how much only time will give. The first part deserves your effort. The second deserves patience, including with yourself.
invitation: Write down the three questions a sceptical stranger would ask about your work, and your honest answer to each. Circle the one answer you could strengthen this month, and leave the other two alone for now.

cross_checks.claim: She started Spanx with her $5,000 savings while keeping her sales job
After failing by phone, she drove to North Carolina and was turned away by the mills
About two weeks later a mill manager called to say he would help, citing his daughters
The idea came in 1998 when she cut the feet off her pantyhose for a party

research_notes: Episode date: no source dates the North Carolina trip. The idea is dated 1998 (Tallahassee Magazine 2007, HuffPost 2011, National Inventors Hall of Fame), the product reached Neiman Marcus in autumn 2000, and Blakely says the prototype took about a year after the mill agreed, so the trip probably fell in 1999; the story says only 'the late 1990s' and approx_date is an inference. The mill: Forbes (2012) places it in Asheboro, North Carolina; Blakely told the 2014 Forbes Under 30 Summit (Entrepreneur) it was a manufacturer in Charlotte; the story names no town. The call came 'two weeks later' (HuffPost, Spanx site, Forbes) or 'two and a half to three weeks later' (Entrepreneur); the story says 'about two weeks'. Daughters: 'two daughters' (Spanx site), 'three daughters' (National Inventors Hall of Fame), 'daughters' (HuffPost, Forbes); the story says 'daughters'. Library: 'seven nights straight' (Forbes) vs 'for weeks at night' (Spanx site); the story says 'evenings'. Patent: she wrote it herself from a book (HuffPost, Forbes) and later had a lawyer help with the claims (Spanx site, National Inventors Hall of Fame); both are given. Leaving her job: she says she quit on 14 October 2000 (HuffPost), Forbes says two weeks before the November 2000 Oprah show, and the Hall of Fame says after it; the story says 'around then'. Outcome figures: Forbes estimated the company's value at $1 billion in 2012 with Blakely as sole owner; first-year sales figures ($4 million per Forbes and the Hall of Fame; her own 'first million' per HuffPost) are not used. The 2021 Blackstone stake is outside the episode. The Confucius passage is a saying addressed to his disciples about office and reputation; it is applied by analogy.
